newsitem.title: BOSNIA: Bosnian Croats block return of Moslem families.
newsitem.headline: Bosnian Croats block return of Moslem families.

text.p: About 200 angry Bosnian Croats, throwing stones and eggs, forced a group of Moslem refugees to cancel a ground-breaking return to their home town on Friday.

The demonstrators blocked the main road to the southern town of Stolac when an escorted bus with nine Moslem families arrived for a long-delayed return to their pre-war homes and parked at a safe distance from the crowd.
Local Croat police formed a cordon to divide the crowd from U.N. relief and police officials and Moslem representatives who were willing to try to talk their way in.

Chanting "no more mosques, no more bowing prayers, no more Moslems", the Croats threw eggs indiscriminately at Moslem officials, U.N. aid workers, officers for the NATO-led peace force and even Croat police.
The crowd was comprised mostly of school children and Croat refugees who had been expelled from central towns which fell to the Moslems during the 1992-1995 Bosnian war.
"I can't return to Kakanj (in central Bosnia), so why should they return here. No one wants them here," said a 65-year-old woman named Ana, who stood by the road watching the crowd.

The nine Moslem families, forced out of Stolac by Croat separatists in 1993, were scheduled to return under supervision of U.N. police monitors and peacekeeping troops in the multinational Stabilisation Force (SFOR).
SFOR had deployed its armoured vehicles all the way from Mostar in the north, from where the bus started and several NATO helicopters hovered around the area.
But no SFOR soldiers tried to disperse the crowd.
The incident dealt another blow to stalled efforts to bring refugees back to their pre-war homes and underlined persistent tensions within the troubled Bosnia's Moslem-Croat federation.

"We believe it's pathetic and an outrage that Moslems are once again prevented from returning to their homes, especially since their return has been discussed with Stolac authorities," said Alexander Ivanko, spokesman for the International Police Task Force (IPTF), which monitors post-war Bosnia.

Croats and Moslems began the Bosnian war as allies but waged a vicious war for territory in 1993. They bowed to U.S. pressure the next year and formed a bi-national federation covering half of Bosnia.
The Dayton peace treaty that ended the Bosnian war in November 1995 guarantees the right of those displaced by fighting to return home.
More than one year since the peace accords were signed, refugee returns have been held up by lingering mistrust and nationalist policies by all the former warring factions.
A Moslem leader said he was not surprised at the blockade.

"I expected something like this as this return has been postponed many times. This is a very bad sign for the future," said Rasim Kadic, minister for refugees in the Croat-Moslem federation. "Obviously, even such a small-scale return as this cannot work," he added.
